newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Sugar - China not buying, premiums stay weak.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar - China not buying, premiums stay weak.

text.p: A lack of Chinese buying has seen Thai white sugar premiums remain weak, and China's sugar factories are hoarding their produce in the hope domestic prices will rise after the Lunar New Year, traders said on Wednesday.

Sugar traders in Tokyo said Thai raw sugar premiums for March/May delivery were quoted at 0.25/0.30 cents (bid/offer) per pound over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on an FOB (free on board) basis.
May/July deliveries were quoted at 0.30/0.35 cents on the New York exchange, they said.
Tokyo trading sources said some Thai traders have been offering raw sugar to Japanese importers for prompt shipment.
"It seems the Thai side wants to ship sugar as soon as possible rather than holding it any longer in warehouses," a sugar trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.
Good harvests in Thailand and Australia, Asia's major producers, will see the regional supply/demand situation continue to soften, they said.
"Iran and Iraq are buying some white sugar, but this will not be big enough to tighten the supply/demand picture," another trader said. "The bottom line is that we need the China factor."
A Chinese trader in Hong Kong who just returned from the southern sugar-producing region of Guangdong, said Chinese processors did not want to sell at present low domestic prices.
"Now the factories are reluctant to sell because they want the price to stabilise at a level where they can at least recover their costs," he said by telephone.
"The factories are holding on to their product, storing it in their warehouses, in the hope that the price will improve after the holiday," he said.
Wholesale prices for white sugar in China have not moved above 3,800 yuan ($458) a tonne for some weeks, as the cane harvest continues and factories are flush with processed sugar.
Break-even point for factories that process cane into coarse granulated white sugar is about 4,000 yuan ($482) a tonne.
Traders in China and Hong Kong polled by Reuters said no movement in prices could be expected at this time of year, when the country closes down for the February 7 Lunar New Year.
"The Spring Festival is very long and holidays are anything from a week to a month in some places, so the market will not change," another Chinese trader said.
Guangdong and neighbouring Guangxi are China's principle sugar-producing provinces. Total sugar production for the current season is expected to be 6.6 million tonnes.
The cane harvest ends in late March, and crushing will continue until around May, after which prices should strengthen.
China's annual sugar demand is around eight million tonnes.
Factories were not immediately concerning themselves with government pronouncements that domestically produced sugar would be bought for central reserves to shore up prices, traders said.
Nor was there any concern about imports as nothing was expected to arrive in China before the middle of the year.
The central government said it would permit sugar imports of 690,000 tonnes, which would include tonnage imported under barter deals with Cuba.
Traders in Tokyo agreed China was unlikely to enter the world market before the second half of 1997, and said authorities in Beijing were closely monitoring sugar imports through Hong Kong.
Traders and producers in the region have said they expect China to import at least 1.5 million tonnes of sugar in 1997.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-7004
-- Eiichiro Tokumoto, Tokyo commodities desk (81-3) 3432-7391
